The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,5)$ and lies on $y=f.$ The point $B$ has coordinates $(5,2)$ and lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ If ${f}^{′}(2)=4,$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(5)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B\,(5,2)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(5)=2.$
We're also told that ${f}^{′}(2)=4.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x}$ and the point $P(4,1)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(1,4)$ is$\,${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(4,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{4}} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(4,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,4)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{8})} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=1+2{e}^{x+1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(3).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(3)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(3) & =x \\ f(x) & =3 \\ 1+2{e}^{x+1} & =3 \\ 2{e}^{x+1} & =2 \\ {e}^{x+1} & =1 \\ x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(3)=-1.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(-1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =1+2{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =2{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={3}^{x}-1.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(8).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(8),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(8)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(8))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(8).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(8)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(8) & =x \\ f(x) & =8 \\ {3}^{x}-1 & =8 \\ {3}^{x} & =9 \\ {3}^{x} & ={3}^{2} \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(8)=2.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={3}^{x}-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{2} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =9\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(8) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(8))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(1).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(1)=x.$ For $x>\frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(1) & =x \\ f(x) & =1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}} & =1 \\ 1 & =\sqrt{2x-1} \\ 1 & =2x-1 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(1)=1.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{(2x-1)^{3/2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =-\frac{1}{(2\cdot 1-1)^{3/2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4).$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $x=0$ since the logarithm is not defined here. Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=5.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4)+\frac{x}{x-4} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4)+\frac{5}{5-4} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={2}^{x}-7.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(9).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(9),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(9)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(9))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(9).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(9)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(9) & =x \\ f(x) & =9 \\ {2}^{x}-7 & =9 \\ {2}^{x} & =16 \\ {2}^{x} & ={2}^{4} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(9)=4.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(4),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={2}^{x}-7 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot {2}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot {2}^{4} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =16\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(9) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(9))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{16\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2-3x}{4+5x}$ and the point $P\left(-1,-5\right)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $\left(-5,-1\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(-1, -5).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2-3x}{4+5x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{22}{(4+5x)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =-22\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(-1, -5)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(-5, -1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ 

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-22)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{22}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table
canonical_examples.problem:
The following table gives the values of $f(x), f'(x),g(x),$ and $g'(x)$ at some points. Find $(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1)$ of the product of functions.

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $g(x)$ | $g'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $3$ | $5$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $f^{-1}(x)g(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(x)=\dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}+g'(x)f^{-1}(x).
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we have

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1) =\dfrac{g(1)}{f'(f^{-1}(1))}+g'(1)f^{-1}(1).
$$

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(1)=2,$ $g(1)=-3,$ $g'(1)=1,$ and $f'(2)=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1}\cdot g)^{′}(1) & =\frac{g(1)}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}+{g}^{′}(1){f}^{-1}(1) \\  & =\frac{-3}{{f}^{′}(2)}+1\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{-3}{-1}+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(2) = x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x}-1 & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x} & =3 \\ {e}^{x} & =1 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f^{-1}(2) = 0.$

Now, we calculate $f'(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3{e}^{x}-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
